segments.text: Euclid's Elements, Book One, Proposition Seven. On the same segment and on the same side, there cannot be constructed two distinct triangles with both pairs of conterminous sides equal. Given segments A C and C B meeting at point C on segment A B, we prove that no distinct point D on the same side can have A D equal to A C and B D equal to B C.

segments.text: For if possible, suppose distinct segments A D and D B on the same side of A B meet at point D, with C A equal to D A and C B equal to D B. Construct segment C D between points C and D, by Postulate One.

segments.text: Since segment A C equals segment A D in isosceles triangle A C D, Proposition Five gives angle A C D equal to angle A D C. By Common Notion Five, the whole is greater than the part: angle A C D is greater than its part, angle D C B, so angle A D C is greater than angle D C B, and the whole angle C D B is much greater than angle D C B. Yet since segment C B equals segment D B in isosceles triangle B C D, Proposition Five gives angle C D B equal to angle D C B, which is a contradiction. Therefore on the same segment A B and on the same side, no distinct point D can have both pairs of conterminous sides equal, as was required to prove.
